*Testing whether W_E encodes non-morphological semantic relations
(antonyms, hypernyms, meronyms, encyclopedic facts) as directional axes.*

### Coherence and Retrieval by Relation

```
Relation               N    Coherence  Retrieval   Reverse     Type
sem:language           4    0.6940     4/4=1.000   4/4=1.000   encyclopedic
sem:currency           4    0.6074     2/4=0.500   3/4=0.750   encyclopedic
morpho:gender         12    0.5414    12/12=1.000  12/12=1.000 derivational
sem:capital            3    0.5165     2/3=0.667   2/3=0.667   encyclopedic
morpho:past           20    0.4600    19/20=0.950  20/20=1.000 inflectional
morpho:plural         20    0.4192    19/20=0.950  20/20=1.000 inflectional
sem:hypernym          20    0.3709     6/20=0.300   0/20=0.000 conceptual
sem:meronym           15    0.2910     4/15=0.267   3/15=0.200 conceptual
sem:antonym_verb      16    0.2726     3/16=0.188   (not tested)  conceptual
sem:antonym_adj       20    0.2702     8/20=0.400   (not tested)  conceptual
```

### Key Finding 1: Language Axis Has Highest Coherence of All (0.694)

  sem:language coherence=0.694 > all morphological axes:
    morpho:gender 0.541, morpho:past 0.460, morpho:plural 0.419

  france->french, germany->german, spain->spanish, russia->russian,
  japan->japanese, italy->italian, poland->polish, sweden->swedish...

  The country->language transformation is the MOST GEOMETRICALLY COHERENT
  relation tested. Probably because:
  (1) Mappings are 1:1 (one country, one primary language)
  (2) European languages follow consistent derivational patterns (-an,-ish,-ese)
  (3) The model was trained on consistent multi-lingual data where this
      relationship is pervasive

  Retrieval: 4/4=100%. Reverse: french->france also 4/4=100%.
  The language axis is perfectly invertible: country->language and
  language->country both work via vector arithmetic.

### Key Finding 2: Hypernym Axis Is One-Way (Reverse = 0/20 = 0%!)

  Hypernym forward: dog+axis -> animal (30% accuracy)
  Hypernym reverse: animal-axis -> dog (0% accuracy)

  The many-to-one structure of hypernymy makes reverse retrieval
  geometrically impossible:
    dog, cat, bird, horse, lion, tiger -> all map to 'animal'
    'animal' minus the axis could recover ANY of them -- but picks none correctly.

  Contrast: morphological axes are BIJECTIVE (one-to-one) --> perfectly
  invertible in both directions.
  Hypernymy is SURJECTIVE (many-to-one) --> not invertible.

  The REVERSIBILITY of an axis predicts whether the underlying relation is
  bijective (invertible) or many-to-one (non-invertible):
    Morphological axes: bijective -> reverse=100%
    Encyclopedic axes (capital, language): ~bijective -> reverse=67-100%
    Conceptual axes (hypernym): many-to-one -> reverse=0%
    Meronym axes: mostly many-to-one -> reverse=20%

### Key Finding 3: Coherence Law Holds for ALL Relation Types

  Coherence predicts retrieval accuracy across morphological AND semantic
  relations (consistent with DC 393):

```
coh=0.694  language      acc=1.000
coh=0.607  currency      acc=0.500  (some currencies multi-token, hurt accuracy)
coh=0.541  gender        acc=1.000
coh=0.517  capital       acc=0.667  (N=3 only, noisy)
coh=0.460  past_tense    acc=0.950
coh=0.419  plural        acc=0.950
coh=0.371  hypernym      acc=0.300
coh=0.291  meronym       acc=0.267
coh=0.273  antonym_verb  acc=0.188
coh=0.270  antonym_adj   acc=0.400
```

  Above coh~0.40: reliable axes (acc > 0.90)
  coh 0.30-0.40: moderate axes (acc 0.30-0.67)
  Below coh~0.30: unreliable axes (acc < 0.30)

### Key Finding 4: Antonyms Are Weakly Encoded (~0.27 coherence)

  adj antonyms (hot/cold, big/small, fast/slow):  coh=0.270, acc=0.400
  verb antonyms (love/hate, buy/sell, win/lose):  coh=0.273, acc=0.188

  Antonyms DO have a consistent directional component (coherence > 0.25)
  but it is much weaker than morphological axes. The antonym axis is not
  a single consistent direction -- 'hot->cold' and 'buy->sell' point in
  quite different parts of W_E.

  The coherence of 0.27 suggests antonymy is PARTIALLY geometric:
  there is a small common 'oppositeness' direction, but most of the
  semantic information is word-specific. This makes sense: antonymy
  is not a systematic morphological rule, it is a semantic relationship
  that varies per domain (temperature, size, commerce, etc.).

### Taxonomy of W_E Relation Types

```
Type                     Coh range   Reversible  Invertible
Derivational (gender)    0.54        yes         yes (bijective)
Inflectional (past,pl)   0.42-0.46   yes         yes (bijective)
Encyclopedic systematic  0.52-0.69   yes         ~yes (near-bijective)
Conceptual (hypernym)    0.37        no          no  (many-to-one)
Conceptual (meronym)     0.29        partial     partial
Antonymy                 0.27        (untested)  (untested)
```

  SYSTEMATIC (morphological + encyclopedic) relations form high-coherence,
  invertible axes.
  CONCEPTUAL (hierarchical, oppositeness) relations form low-coherence,
  non-invertible axes.

### Part 2: Antonym Relation Is Perfectly Symmetric

  cos(hot->cold axis, cold->hot axis) = -1.0000 (EXACT)

  The antonym transformation is the SAME geometric direction regardless
  of which end you start from:
    hot -> cold: axis = d
    cold -> hot: axis = -d (exact negation)

  This perfect symmetry is expected from geometry:
  if emb(cold) = emb(hot) + d, then emb(hot) = emb(cold) - d.
  No asymmetry -- both ends of an antonym pair are equidistant from
  the midpoint along the same axis.

  Contrast: hypernym (coh=0.371) has ZERO reverse accuracy -- it is
  fundamentally asymmetric because it is not a bijective relation.

### Part 3: What the Universal Antonym Axis Encodes

  Per-pair cosine similarity with universal axis:
  Highest: wide/narrow=0.408, strong/weak=0.392, big/small=0.364,
           deep/shallow=0.370, fast/slow=0.338
  Lowest:  easy/hard=0.107, young/old=0.158, open/closed=0.204

  The axis ACTUALLY encodes a MAGNITUDE/INTENSITY dimension:

```
Positive pole (low magnitude, passive):  weak, slow, quiet, soft, short, small, light, poor
Negative pole (high magnitude, active):  big, rich, bright, fast, heavy, strong, loud, tall
```

  This is NOT a pure antonymy axis. It is the INTENSITY/MAGNITUDE
  dimension of adjective meaning.
  'Big' and 'rich' are both high-magnitude properties, so they project
  negatively. 'Small' and 'weak' are low-magnitude, projecting positively.

  The antonym axis captures the shared semantic dimension of SCALE within
  the antonym pairs (big/small, fast/slow, heavy/light), but NOT the
  domain-specific content (temperature, social status, etc.).

### Reconciliation with DC 380 ('Antonymy Not Functional')

  DC 380 concluded that antonymy is not encoded as a functional directional
  axis. Day 267 refines this:

  DC 380 was RIGHT that a universal antonym axis fails: coh=0.27, acc=0.40.

  Day 267 shows that DOMAIN-SPECIFIC antonym axes ARE functional:
    speed:  coh=0.756, rev=3/3=100%
    social: coh=0.428, fwd=6/6=100%, rev=6/6=100%

  Antonymy is not a SINGLE geometric transformation. It is a FAMILY of
  domain-specific transformations:
    - The temperature axis (hot<->cold)
    - The speed axis (fast<->slow)
    - The size axis (big<->small)
    - The social axis (rich<->poor)
    etc.

  These are different axes. Mixing them produces the low-coherence
  'universal antonym axis'. Each individually has high coherence and
  full invertibility.

### Connection to the Coherence Law

  The coherence law predicts that axes with coherence > 0.40 have high
  retrieval accuracy. Day 267 confirms this for domain-specific antonym axes:
    speed coh=0.756 -> rev=100%
    social coh=0.428 -> fwd=rev=100%
    quality coh=0.402 -> fwd=rev=75%

  The 'universal antonym axis' failure is not a fundamental limit of
  antonymy -- it is a consequence of mixing multiple high-coherence
  domain axes into one low-coherence universal axis.

Social antonyms: coh=0.428, fwd=6/6=100%, rev=6/6=100%.
Universal axis encodes MAGNITUDE/INTENSITY, not pure antonymy.

## Day 269 — The Country Axis: Second-Order Structure in W_E

*Extract the shared 'country axis' from PCA of the 3 encyclopedic axes.
What does it encode? Test second-order geometric structure.*

### Part 1: SVD of Encyclopedic Axis Matrix

```
Singular values of [capital_axis; language_axis; currency_axis]:
  S = [1.218, 0.919, 0.819]
  PC1 explains 49.5% of variance in encyclopedic subspace

Projections of enc axes onto country_axis (PC1):
  capital  -> -0.680
  language -> -0.774
  currency -> -0.650
```

  All three projections are NEGATIVE and substantial (0.65-0.77).
  The country_axis points FROM national properties TOWARD country names
  (it is the SOURCE end of all three encyclopedic axes).

### Part 2: Country Axis IS the 'Country Name' Dimension

  The 40 highest-projecting tokens on country_axis are almost ALL
  country names:

```
Top projections (positive = country names):
  germany(+0.522), france(+0.517), japan(+0.428), china(+0.419),
  Germany(+0.409), mexico(+0.404), india(+0.357), canada(+0.346),
  australia(+0.344), France(+0.343), Ireland(+0.314), Norway(+0.281)...

Lowest projections (negative = national properties):
  real(-0.153), peso(-0.132), Spanish(-0.126), English(-0.122),
  paris(-0.121), French(-0.116), Chinese(-0.115), yuan(-0.112),
  yen(-0.109), Welsh(-0.106), Russian(-0.103)...
```

  POSITIVE pole: country names (france, germany, japan, china, mexico...)
  NEGATIVE pole: national properties (currencies: real/peso/yuan/yen;
                                      languages: Spanish/French/Chinese;
                                      capitals: paris)

  The country_axis is the W_E dimension that separates the CONCEPT of a
  country (as an entity) from its ATTRIBUTES (language, capital, currency).

### Part 3: Adding Country Axis to Country Gives OTHER Countries

  france + country_axis -> germany, France, France...
  The country_axis points INTO the country cluster -- adding it to a
  country embedding moves DEEPER into the country-name region.
  To retrieve national properties, we need to SUBTRACT: country - axis.

  This confirms the geometry:
    country vector = high positive projection on country_axis
    property vector = negative projection on country_axis
    enc_axis = direction FROM country cluster TO property cluster
               = -country_axis + domain_specific_component

### Part 4: Domain-Specific Residuals After Removing Country Component

  After subtracting the shared country_axis component from each enc axis,
  the residual axes point directly at their target categories:

```
capital residual  NN: [berlin, paris, Berlin, Berlin, Paris]  ✓ capitals!
language residual NN: [french, japanese, chinese, german, spanish]  ✓ languages!
currency residual NN: [real, yen, peso, yuan, Real]  ✓ currencies!
```

  The domain residuals are ANTI-CORRELATED with each other:
    cos(capital_residual, language_residual) = -0.501
    cos(capital_residual, currency_residual) = -0.512
    cos(language_residual, currency_residual) = -0.487

  After removing the shared country component, the domain axes point in
  OPPOSITE directions from each other -- they discriminate between
  capital vs language vs currency in the property space.

### Geometric Structure of Encyclopedic Knowledge

  Each encyclopedic axis decomposes as:

```
enc_axis = -(0.65-0.77) * country_axis + domain_specific_component
```

  The country_axis itself identifies the 'country' semantic region of W_E.
  From any country embedding:
    country - enc_axis_capital   -> capital city
    country - enc_axis_language  -> national language
    country - enc_axis_currency  -> national currency
  (minus because enc_axis points FROM country TO property)

  The domain_specific_components are anti-correlated: walking AWAY from the
  capital direction takes you toward the currency/language region, etc.
  This is the SECOND-ORDER STRUCTURE: a 3-dimensional 'national facts'
  subspace with country_axis as one dimension and capital/language/currency
  directions as the other two.

### Connection to TruthSpace Hypothesis

  The country axis is NOT hand-coded. It emerged from the PCA of three
  independently computed semantic axes. W_E spontaneously organised
  national facts into a structured subspace with:
    1. A 'country entity' dimension (what kind of thing is this?)
    2. Domain-specific property dimensions (what is its X?)

  This is exactly the kind of emergent geometric structure predicted by the
  TruthSpace hypothesis: knowledge is not stored as flat key-value pairs,
  but as geometric relationships in a structured space.

---

*Day 269: Country axis discovered via PCA of 3 encyclopedic enc axes.
Country axis = highest-projecting words are COUNTRY NAMES (france, germany...).
Negative pole = national properties (currencies, languages, capitals).
Domain residuals after removing country component correctly NN to:
  capital residual -> berlin/paris/Berlin/Paris
  language residual -> french/japanese/chinese/german/spanish
  currency residual -> real/yen/peso/yuan
Residuals are anti-correlated (~-0.50 pairwise).
Second-order structure: 3D 'national facts' subspace = country_axis + 2 domain axes.

## Day 270 — Second-Order Axes: Inflectional and Category

*Testing DC 404's prediction: second-order axes can be extracted by PCA
from first-order axis clusters. Testing inflectional axis (PCA of 4 morpho
axes) and hypernym PC1 axis.*

### Part 1: Inflectional Axis (PCA of adj/superlative/plural/past)

```
SVD: S = [1.306, 0.970, 0.907, 0.729]
PC1 explains 42.7% of variance in morphological axis subspace

Projections of morpho axes onto inflectional PC1:
  adj_degree  -> -0.767
  superlative -> -0.769
  plural      -> -0.534
  past_tense  -> -0.492
```

  All four morpho axes project NEGATIVELY onto inflectional PC1 (similar
  to enc axes projecting negatively onto country axis). PC1 points TOWARD
  the SOURCE end (base forms) of all morphological transformations.

  The positive pole of inflectional axis is NOT inflected forms -- it is
  function words and punctuation (, . and " in 1 a 2 - ...).
  This is the markedness/frequency gradient: least marked tokens (high
  frequency function words) sit at the positive end.

  CRITICAL FINDING: Inflected forms consistently project LOWER than base:

```
Pair         inflected  base    inflected < base?
walk/ed      -0.155     +0.062  YES
cats/cat     -0.138     +0.074  YES
bigger/big   -0.313     +0.192  YES
fastest/fast -0.339     +0.187  YES
went/go      -0.060     +0.164  YES
mice/mouse   -0.135     -0.026  YES
children/child -0.011   +0.057  YES
better/good  -0.145     +0.192  YES
played/play  -0.127     +0.109  YES
────────────────────────────────────────
Inflected > Base: 0/14 (base ALWAYS projects higher)
```

  The inflectional axis is a MARKEDNESS axis: less marked (base, function)
  words project positively; more marked (inflected) forms project negatively.
  It does not cleanly classify 'inflected/base' on its own, but combined
  with projection threshold it gives 100% correct ordering.

### Part 2: Hypernym PC1 (PCA of 20 hypernym chords)

```
SVD of 20 hypernym chord vectors:
  S = [1.711, 0.904, 0.837, 0.773, 0.749]
  PC1 explains 28.0% of hypernym chord variance
```

  Hypernym PC1 is an 'ANIMAL-NESS' axis, not a generic 'specific vs general':

```
Top positive projections (specific animals):
  bear(+0.146), wolf(+0.138), tiger(+0.136), lion(+0.128), cat(+0.114)

Highly negative (generic concept 'animal'):
  animal(-0.865)  Animal(-0.682)  animals(-0.621)  creature(-0.258)
  object(-0.178)  organism(-0.169)  entity(-0.103)  thing(-0.040)
```

  'animal' alone projects at -0.865, far more extreme than any other word.
  The PC1 of the hypernym chords is dominated by the contrast between
  'animal' (extreme negative) and specific large animals (moderate positive).

  Non-animal specifics (dog=-0.005, hammer=+0.012, chair=+0.012) are near zero
  -- they don't participate in the animal-ness axis.

  This is narrower than the country axis (which captured ALL country names).
  The hypernym PC1 only captures the DOMINANT hypernym relation in the training
  set (animal), not a universal 'specific vs general' axis.

### Part 3: Second-Order Axes Are Mutually Near-Orthogonal

```
cos(inflectional, country)  = -0.015  ~0 (orthogonal)
cos(inflectional, hypernym) = -0.010  ~0 (orthogonal)
cos(country, hypernym)      = -0.031  ~0 (orthogonal)
```

  The three second-order axes are mutually near-orthogonal, exactly as
  the first-order axes are (|cos| < 0.05 in 60% of cases, DC 403).
  The hierarchy of axes is structurally consistent across levels:
  first-order axes are mostly orthogonal, second-order axes are mostly
  orthogonal, and second-order is orthogonal to first-order.

### Why Country Axis Works Better Than Inflectional Axis

  Country axis PC1 explained 49.5% of enc variance and cleanly separated
  country names from properties.
  Inflectional axis PC1 explains 42.7% of morph variance but separates
  function words (positive) from inflected forms (negative) -- not clean.

  The difference: the 3 enc axes share the SAME source type (country names),
  so their common component is specifically 'country-ness'.
  The 4 morpho axes do NOT share the same source type -- adj axes come from
  adjectives, plural/past from nouns/verbs. Their shared component is a
  broader 'morphological marking' direction that aligns with the general
  frequency/markedness gradient of W_E.

  PREDICTION: If we compute the inflectional axis from only NOUN plural axes
  (shared source type: common nouns), we would get a cleaner 'noun-ness' axis.

Only captures dominant hypernym target; not a universal specific-vs-general axis.

## Day 271 — DC 405 Prediction Test: Same-Source-Type Second-Order Axes

*Directly testing DC 405's key claim: same-source-type second-order axes
should be cleaner than mixed-source-type axes. Testing adj+sup (adjective
sources) vs plu+pst (noun+verb sources, mixed).*

### adj-only Second-Order Axis (adj_degree + superlative)

```
SVD: S = [1.212, 0.729]  ->  PC1 explains 73.4% of variance
Projections: adj_degree=-0.857, superlative=-0.857  (both identical!)
```

  Category mean projections on adj_base axis:

```
adj_base (base forms)  +0.159   ← highest content word category
adj_comp (comparative) -0.349   ← large negative gap
adj_sup  (superlative) -0.386   ← even more negative
nouns                  +0.004   ← near zero
verbs                  +0.039   ← near zero
func words             +0.127   ← still high (markedness gradient)
```

  adj_base (+0.159) vs adj_comp (-0.349): GAP = 0.508 (the largest seen)
  adj_base > nouns? TRUE
  Negative pole contains superlatives and comparatives:
    weakest, louder, highest, toughest, quickest, tougher, quicker,
    poorest, brightest, nicer, darkest, wealthiest, widest, tallest...

  Function words still dominate positive pole (, ( and . in high a...)
  -- but adjective bases (+0.159) sit significantly ABOVE nouns (+0.004)
  and verbs (+0.039), confirming partial discrimination.

### Four-Scenario Comparison

```
Axis combination         PC1%   adj_base  adj_comp  nouns   DC405_pred
adj+sup  (same POS)      73.4%  +0.159    -0.349    +0.004  CONFIRMED
  adj_base > nouns: YES                                      ✓
plu+pst  (noun+verb)     58.8%  +0.034    -0.102    +0.092  CONFIRMED
  adj_base > nouns: NO  (nouns=0.092 > adj=0.034)           ✓ (wrong axis)
adj+plu  (adj+noun)      59.4%  +0.090    -0.366    +0.068  partial
  adj_base > nouns: YES                                      ✓
all 4    (mixed)         42.7%  +0.138    -0.317    +0.046  partial
  adj_base > nouns: YES                                      ✓
```

  DC 405 CONFIRMED:
  - Same-source-type (adj+sup) gives HIGHEST PC1 variance (73.4% vs 42-59%)
  - Same-source-type gives LARGEST adj_base vs adj_comp separation (0.508)
  - Mixed-source (plu+pst) REVERSES the adj_base > nouns relationship
    (nouns=+0.092 > adj_base=+0.034) -- the axis captures noun-ness, not adj-ness

### Why Function Words Still Dominate Positive Pole

  Even with same-source-type (adj+sup), function words (+0.127) still
  rank near adjective bases (+0.159). This is because common adjectives
  (big, fast, long, high, deep, hard, clear, clean) share a frequency/
  position profile with short function words in training data.

  The country axis is uniquely clean because country NAMES form a specific
  named-entity cluster in W_E that does NOT overlap with function words.
  Common adjective BASE forms are not named entities -- they are ordinary
  content words that blend into the general high-frequency vocabulary.

  CONCLUSION: DC 405's prediction is verified, but the country axis is
  uniquely privileged because country names are a named-entity class with
  a distinct geometric footprint. Second-order axes for grammatical POS
  categories are weaker because POS boundaries in W_E are gradient, not sharp.

### Plural Axis as POS Classifier

  Directly testing plural axis as singular/plural noun discriminator:
```
noun_plural  +0.187   (positive pole)
adj_base     -0.006   (near zero)
func_words   -0.078   (negative)
nouns        -0.104   (negative! base nouns project negative)
verbs        -0.039   (near zero)
```
  The plural axis correctly identifies PLURAL nouns at positive end and
  SINGULAR nouns at negative end -- it IS a plural/singular discriminator.
  This is the first-order axis being used directly (not second-order).

Negative pole: German, British, French, Italian, Japanese, American...
Category means: person=+0.239, city=+0.065, country=+0.019, adj=-0.004, func=-0.039.
cos(person, country) = +0.147 (partial overlap = shared named-entity component).

## Day 273 — Third-Order Named-Entity Axis: Negative Result

*Attempting to extract a 3rd-order 'named entity vs common word' axis
via PCA of [country_axis, person_axis, city_axis]. Result: the PCA
captures city vs country discrimination, NOT a universal NE axis.
The prediction partially failed due to city-country semantic entanglement.*

### City Axis Construction

```
City->country axis coherence:   0.775
City->continent axis coherence: 0.772
City axis PC1 variance: 71.1%

cos(city_axis, country_axis) = -0.548  !! ANTI-CORRELATED
cos(city_axis, person_axis)  = +0.056  (near-orthogonal)
```

  City axis ANTI-CORRELATES with country axis (cos=-0.548).
  WHY: City→country relations point FROM cities TOWARD countries.
  Country axis (from capital/language/currency enc axes) points FROM
  national properties TOWARD country names (positive = country names).
  These happen to point in OPPOSITE directions in W_E because cities
  and country names are on OPPOSITE ENDS of the same geographic axis.

### Third-Order Axis: City vs Country, Not NE vs Common

```
NE axis = PCA of [country_axis, person_axis, city_axis]
PC1 variance: 51.9%
Projections: country=-0.890  person=-0.162  city=+0.859
```

  The NE axis is dominated by the CONTRAST between city_axis and
  country_axis, not a shared NE direction. It is essentially the
  city axis with inverted country axis.

```
Positive pole (NE axis): paris, berlin, Paris, Berlin, London,
  Beijing, Nairobi, Moscow, Boston, Miami, Madrid...
Negative pole:           france, germany, europe, Germany, France,
  Italy, Europe, Spain, china, japan, Ireland, canada...
```

  Category means:
    cities     +0.150  (positive)
    countries  -0.276  (negative -- strong contrast!)
    persons    -0.037  (near zero)
    companies  -0.014  (near zero)
    adj bases  +0.008  (near zero)
    func words +0.003  (near zero)

  The axis is a CITY-vs-COUNTRY discriminator. At threshold=0.10:
    cities:  2/5 above (40%)  countries: 0/10 above (0%)
    persons: 0/15 above        animals:   0/10 above

### Why the Third-Order Axis Failed

  The country_axis and city_axis are semantically ENTANGLED:
  - City embeddings live near country embeddings in W_E
  - The direction from country_emb to city_emb IS a meaningful relation
  - Therefore city_axis ~ -country_axis (anti-correlated by cos=-0.548)

  When we PCA [country, person, city], the city-country anti-correlation
  dominates the first singular value (explains 51.9%), producing the
  city-country contrast, not a shared NE direction.

  For a true third-order NE axis we need SEMANTICALLY INDEPENDENT
  named-entity categories. Countries and cities are NOT independent --
  they share the geographic/geopolitical semantic domain.

### Correct Approach for Third-Order NE Axis

  Required: second-order axes from semantically INDEPENDENT categories:
    - country_axis (geopolitical entities)
    - person_axis  (famous people -- INDEPENDENT of geography)
    - element_axis (chemical elements -- independent of both)
    - species_axis (animal/plant species -- independent)
    - company_axis (corporations -- independent)

  These categories do NOT have systematic first-order relations to each
  other in the training pairs, so their second-order axes will not be
  anti-correlated. Their shared component (all are named entities) will
  be the actual third-order NE direction.

  cos(person_axis, country_axis) = +0.147 (partial overlap)
  This 0.147 IS the genuine 'named entity' shared component.
  To extract it cleanly we need more independent NE category axes to
  average out the domain-specific components.

---

*Day 273: Third-order NE axis test -- NEGATIVE RESULT.
city_axis anti-correlates with country_axis (cos=-0.548): geographic entanglement.
PCA of [country, person, city] yields city-vs-country discriminator, not NE axis.
Category means: cities=+0.150, countries=-0.276, persons=-0.037 (not universal NE).
Correct approach: use semantically INDEPENDENT NE categories (elements, species, companies).
DC 408 written.*

## Day 274 — Third-Order Named-Entity Axis (4 Independent Categories)

*Testing DC 408 plan: PCA of [country_axis, person_axis, element_axis, company_axis].
All four are semantically independent second-order axes. Result: the third-order
NE axis WORKS but is inverted (named entities = negative pole).*

### Four Second-Order Axes: Near-Orthogonal

```
Element axis:  element->type coh=0.515, element->element coh=0.784
               element axis PC1=57.9%
Company axis:  company->industry coh=0.434, company->product coh=0.408

Cross-category cosines (all near zero -- independent!):
  cos(country, person)  = +0.155  (small overlap from nationality)
  cos(country, element) = +0.036  (near-zero)
  cos(element, person)  = +0.087  (near-zero)
  cos(company, country) = +0.007  (orthogonal!)
  cos(company, person)  = +0.067  (near-zero)
  cos(company, element) = +0.021  (orthogonal!)
```

  The four second-order axes are nearly mutually orthogonal, confirming
  they represent genuinely independent semantic domains.

### Third-Order NE Axis

```
NE axis = PCA of [country, person, element, company]
SVD: S = [1.100, 0.998, 0.984, 0.909]
PC1 variance: 30.3%  (low -- 4 nearly orthogonal axes share little variance)

Projections onto NE axis:
  country = -0.624   person = -0.735
  element = -0.438   company= -0.299
  -- ALL FOUR project NEGATIVELY --
```

  All four second-order axes project negatively onto PC1.
  Therefore the NE axis points FROM attributes TOWARD named entities
  (same sign convention as previous axes: enc axes pointed FROM countries
  TOWARD properties; PC1 pointed FROM properties TOWARD countries).

  NAMED ENTITIES are at the NEGATIVE POLE of the NE axis.

### NE Axis Positive and Negative Poles

  Positive pole (attribute direction):
```
British(+0.368), French(+0.316), German(+0.301), Italian(+0.270),
American(+0.260), Japanese(+0.248), Spanish(+0.248), Russian(+0.240),
English(+0.233), Chinese(+0.231), Dutch(+0.221), Australian(+0.220),
Greek(+0.218), Irish(+0.215), Canadian(+0.214), European(+0.204),
Swedish(+0.202), metal(+0.168), element(+0.191), elements(+0.172)
```

  Negative pole (named entity direction):
```
germany(-0.303), france(-0.288), mexico(-0.287), china(-0.267),
Lenin(-0.263), Tesla(-0.262), india(-0.256), nigeria(-0.253),
japan(-0.252), Hitler(-0.250), Goku(-0.249), Dumbledore(-0.248),
Mandela(-0.246), pakistan(-0.245), Antarctica(-0.243), canada(-0.239)
```

### Category Means: NE Axis IS a Universal NE Discriminator

```
Category          mean_proj   Role
func words        +0.080      positive (common words)
adj bases         +0.018      near-zero (common words)
cities            -0.077      negative (named entity class)
elements          -0.116      negative (named entity class)
companies         -0.158      negative (named entity class)
persons           -0.211      negative (named entity class)
countries         -0.253      negative (named entity class)
```

  Named entities score NEGATIVE, common words score POSITIVE/NEAR-ZERO.
  The NE axis correctly separates named-entity classes from common words!

  Filter at threshold < -0.05 correctly identifies NE tokens.
  Filter at threshold > +0.05 correctly identifies common words (func=80%).

### Why Only 30.3% PC1 Variance

  The four second-order axes are nearly orthogonal (all cross-cosines <0.16).
  Their shared component (the NE direction) is WEAK -- only 30.3% vs 49-52%
  for single-category second-order axes.

  The NE axis works but is NOISY: the four domains contribute roughly
  equally (singular values 1.10, 1.00, 0.98, 0.91 -- nearly equal).
  This means the four domains have EQUAL shares of the total variance;
  the first PC explains only 30% because there is no dominant shared direction.

  The NE direction exists but is spread across all four domains equally,
  not concentrated in one. This is expected: countries, persons, elements,
  and companies are similar in 'named-entity-ness' but differ in all
  other semantic dimensions.

### Summary: Third-Order NE Axis Confirmed (with Inverted Sign)

  DC 408 plan succeeded: semantically INDEPENDENT NE categories yield a
  genuine NE axis. The axis inverts relative to what was predicted
  (negative pole = named entities), but the separation is real.

  Three-level hierarchy confirmed:
    1st order: enc/morph axes (capital, language, currency, plural, ...)
    2nd order: country_axis, person_axis, element_axis, company_axis
    3rd order: NE axis (shared direction across all named-entity categories)

---

Named entities = negative pole: countries=-0.253, persons=-0.211, companies=-0.158, elements=-0.116.
Common words = positive/near-zero: func=+0.080, adj=+0.018.
Positive pole = nationality adjectives + type words (British, French, German, element, metal).
NE axis is a valid universal NE filter (NE score < -0.05 = named entity).

## Day 275 — NE Axis Precision/Recall on Full Vocabulary

*Testing whether the NE axis works as a universal named-entity filter
across the entire 151,936-token vocabulary. Result: NEGATIVE.
The axis correctly scores trained NE categories but fails as a universal
classifier. The vocabulary mean is already -0.085 (shifted negative),
and at every threshold cap_recall ~= lower_FP (no discrimination).*

### Score Distribution on Full Vocabulary

```
mean=-0.085  std=0.047
min=-0.303   max=+0.368
p25=-0.110   p50=-0.084   p75=-0.058   p95=-0.014
```

  THE ENTIRE VOCABULARY MEAN IS -0.085 (negative!).
  The median is also -0.084. More than 75% of tokens score below -0.058.
  The distribution is already negative-shifted -- not centred at zero.
  An absolute threshold does not discriminate NE from non-NE.

### Threshold Analysis: No Discrimination

```
Threshold  Retrieved  Cap+alpha   Lower-alpha  Other
<-0.10     51,219(34%) 7,134(14%)  26,593(52%)  24,343(47%)
<-0.15     11,312( 7%)   779( 7%)   3,073(27%)   8,221(73%)
<-0.20      4,701( 3%)   104( 2%)     327( 7%)   4,372(93%)
```

  At threshold < -0.15: 73% of retrieved tokens are 'Other'
  (Unicode fragments, CJK characters, subword pieces, punctuation).
  Only 7% are capitalized-alpha (NE-like).

  At threshold < -0.20: 93% are Other. The NE axis picks up
  non-alphabetic BPE fragments more strongly than named entity tokens!

### Recall vs FP: No Separation

```
Threshold  cap_recall  lower_FP   Discriminating?
<-0.05     77.4%       79.4%      NO (FP > recall)
<-0.10     26.9%       30.7%      NO (FP > recall)
<-0.15      2.9%        3.6%      NO (FP > recall)
<-0.20      0.4%        0.4%      NO (equal)
```

  At EVERY threshold, lower-alpha false-positive rate >= cap-recall.
  The NE axis does NOT preferentially retrieve capitalized/NE tokens
  over lowercase common words in the full vocabulary.

### Why the NE Axis Fails as a Universal Filter

  1. DISTRIBUTION SHIFT: The vocabulary mean is -0.085. The whole
     vocabulary is shifted negative. There is no clear positive/negative
     separation.

  2. BPE FRAGMENT NOISE: Qwen's 151k tokenizer contains tens of thousands
     of non-alphabetic tokens (CJK characters, Unicode fragments, subword
     pieces). These score very negative, dominating the retrieved set at
     strict thresholds.

  3. CAPITALISATION != NE: Many proper nouns in Qwen are stored as
     lowercase tokens (france, germany, japan...). Many capitalised tokens
     are not NEs (sentence-initial words, acronyms, all-caps technical terms).
     The heuristic breaks down.

  4. NE AXIS IS RELATIVE, NOT ABSOLUTE: The trained NE categories score
     0.08-0.17 below the MEAN, but the axis is not a clean categorical
     split. It captures a gradient, not a binary distinction.

### What DOES Work: Relative Scoring Within Known Categories

  The NE axis correctly RANKS specific known NE categories:
    countries:  -0.253   persons: -0.211   companies: -0.158
    elements:   -0.116   cities:  -0.077   adj bases: +0.018
    func words: +0.080

  This relative ranking is real and consistent. But it only works when
  comparing WORD-LEVEL tokens against each other, not when applied to
  the entire BPE vocabulary including subword fragments.

  Practical implication: the NE axis is useful as a RE-RANKER among
  candidate word tokens (e.g. filter to alphabetic tokens first, then
  rank by NE score), not as a threshold-based universal filter.

---

*Day 275: NE axis full-vocab precision/recall -- NEGATIVE RESULT.
Vocab mean = -0.085 (whole vocab skews negative). At every threshold:
  cap_recall (capitalized NE-like tokens) < lower_FP (lowercase words).
At thr < -0.15: 73% of retrieved tokens are Unicode/BPE fragments, not NEs.
NE axis works as a RE-RANKER within alphabetic token candidates,
not as a universal threshold-based NE filter.
DC 410 written.*

## Day 276 — Compositional Axis Chaining

*Testing the TruthSpace hypothesis that multi-hop geometric retrieval
works by additive axis composition. Result: NEGATIVE for additive
stacking; PARTIAL for classic analogy arithmetic.*

### Single-Hop Accuracy (calibrated scales)

```
capital axis:     scale=0.25  acc=2/8  (25%)   coh=0.775
language axis:    scale=0.25  acc=4/5  (80%)   coh=0.694
person->nat axis: scale=0.41  acc=9/20 (45%)   coh=0.499
```

  Note: capital axis low accuracy (2/8) due to few single-token
  country+capital pairs. Language axis is most reliable (80%).

### Experiment 1: Language Axis Generalisation to Cities

  Does city_emb + scale * language_axis -> city's language?
  Result: 0/12 (0%).

  Retrieved: Paris (for paris), Berlin (for berlin), ROME (for rome)...
  The language axis retrieves the CAPITALISED form of the same city,
  not the language. The axis is SPECIFIC to country embeddings.
  It does not generalise from countries to cities.

  Conclusion: first-order axes are SOURCE-TYPE SPECIFIC. The language
  axis encodes 'where france lives relative to french', not a universal
  'geographic entity -> its language' direction.

### Experiment 2: Additive Two-Hop Chain

  country_emb + scale_cap*cap_axis + scale_lan*lan_axis -> language?
  Direct language (single hop): 4/12 (33%)
  Two-hop additive sum:          3/12 (25%)  -- WORSE!

  Adding the capital axis INTERFERES with language retrieval.
  The two axes partially cancel, overshooting the language region.

### Experiment 3: Three-Hop Additive Chain

  person_emb + nat_axis + dem_cty_axis + lan_axis -> language?
  Result: 0/12 (0%).

  All results converged to 'germany' (dominant country in training pairs).
  Three additive axes completely overshoot. The sum of three scaled
  direction vectors has no anchor in the actual target region.

### Experiment 4: Analogy Arithmetic

  A:B::C:? => C_emb + (B_emb - A_emb) = ?
```
france:paris  :: germany:berlin  -> got Paris     MISS (capitalised duplicate)
france:french :: germany:german  -> HIT
france:french :: japan:japanese  -> HIT
Einstein:German :: Newton:British -> got German   MISS (same word)
Einstein:German :: Kepler:German  -> HIT (trivial: same nationality)
Einstein:physicist :: Darwin:biologist -> got physicists  MISS (morphology)
Analogy accuracy: 3/11 (27%)
```

  Works for LANGUAGE analogies (france:french::japan:japanese).
  Fails for CAPITAL analogies (displacement france->paris is city-specific).
  Fails for PERSON analogies (Newton:British is swamped by Newton's own vector).

### Key Findings

  1. Axes are SOURCE-TYPE SPECIFIC: language axis from country->language
     pairs does not generalise to city embeddings. Axes encode relations
     for the EXACT SOURCE TYPE used in construction, not for semantically
     related types.

  2. ADDITIVE COMPOSITION FAILS for multi-hop: stacking 2-3 axes by
     addition overshoots/interferes. Two axes hurt retrieval (33%->25%);
     three axes collapse to a single dominant anchor.

  3. ANALOGY ARITHMETIC works partially (27%): only for cases where
     the single-hop displacement vector is large relative to both the
     source word's absolute position and token-specific noise.

  4. Language axis is most composition-friendly (works in analogy test).
     Capital axis fails analogy because city embeddings are too
     city-specific (Paris != generic French capital representation).

### Implication: Sequential Chaining Required

  The correct multi-hop algorithm is SEQUENTIAL, not simultaneous:
  1. Apply axis 1: emb(person) + scale*ax_nat -> retrieve intermediate
  2. Look up the intermediate embedding via NN search
  3. Apply axis 2: emb(intermediate) + scale*ax2 -> retrieve next hop

  Day 277 test: sequential chaining vs additive chaining.

---

*Day 276: Compositional axis chaining -- NEGATIVE for additive stacking.
Language axis does NOT generalise from countries to cities (0/12).
Two-hop additive chain: 3/12 (25%) WORSE than single-hop 4/12 (33%).
Three-hop additive chain: 0/12 (0%) -- converges to dominant training anchor.
Analogy arithmetic: 3/11 (27%) -- works for language, fails for capital/person.
Axes are source-type specific; additive composition overshoots.
Correct approach: SEQUENTIAL chaining (retrieve intermediate, then continue).
DC 411 written.*

## Day 277 — Sequential Axis Chaining

*Testing sequential (NN-grounded) chaining vs additive stacking.
Result: DECISIVE WIN for sequential. 2-hop: 42% seq vs 33% add.
3-hop: 50% seq vs 0% add. Sequential EXCEEDS the 12% product-of-singles
prediction, revealing positive hop correlation.*

### Single-hop Baselines

```
capital:     coh=0.775  scale=0.25  acc= 2/8  (25%)
language:    coh=0.694  scale=0.25  acc= 4/5  (80%)
person->nat: coh=0.499  scale=0.41  acc= 9/20 (45%)
demonym->cty:coh=0.787  scale=0.56  acc= 5/15 (33%)
```

### Sequential 2-Hop: person -[nat]-> nationality -[dem]-> country

```
Einstein     nat->German    [HIT]  seq_cty=germany     [HIT]  add=germany     [HIT]
Newton       nat->Newton    [---]  seq_cty=Newton      [---]  add=Newton      [---]
Darwin       nat->German    [---]  seq_cty=germany     [---]  add=germany     [---]
Kepler       nat->German    [HIT]  seq_cty=germany     [HIT]  add=germany     [HIT]
Gauss        nat->gauss     [---]  seq_cty=germany     [HIT]  add=gauss       [---]
Turing       nat->German    [---]  seq_cty=germany     [---]  add=germany     [---]
Napoleon     nat->French    [HIT]  seq_cty=france      [HIT]  add=france      [HIT]
Caesar       nat->German    [---]  seq_cty=germany     [---]  add=germany     [---]
Aristotle    nat->Greek     [HIT]  seq_cty=Greece      [---]  add=germany     [---]
Mozart       nat->Austrian  [HIT]  seq_cty=Austria     [---]  add=germany     [---]
Marx         nat->German    [HIT]  seq_cty=germany     [HIT]  add=germany     [HIT]

Nat retrieval (step 1):     6/12 (50%)
Sequential 2-hop:           5/12 (42%)  -- BETTER than additive!
Additive 2-hop:             4/12 (33%)
```

  Key observation: Gauss gets wrong nat ('gauss') but still reaches
  germany via sequential (emb('gauss')+dem_axis -> germany). Gauss's
  embedding is close enough to German surnames that the demonym axis
  retrieves the right country even from an incorrect intermediate.

  Aristotle and Mozart: nat retrieved correctly (Greek, Austrian) but
  seq_cty fails (Greece/Austria not lowercased or missing from axis).
  Case mismatch: dem_cty axis trained on lowercase ('greece','austria')
  but retrieved tokens are 'Greece','Austria' (capitalised).

### Sequential 3-Hop: person -[nat]-> -[dem]-> country -[lan]-> language

```
Einstein   nat=German    cty=germany   seq_lan=german    [HIT]  add=germany  [---]
Newton     nat=Newton    cty=Newton    seq_lan=Newton    [---]  add=Newton   [---]
Darwin     nat=German    cty=germany   seq_lan=german    [---]  add=germany  [---]
Kepler     nat=German    cty=germany   seq_lan=german    [HIT]  add=germany  [---]
Gauss      nat=gauss     cty=germany   seq_lan=german    [HIT]  add=gauss    [---]
Napoleon   nat=French    cty=france    seq_lan=french    [HIT]  add=france   [---]
Aristotle  nat=Greek     cty=Greece    seq_lan=Greek     [---]  add=germany  [---]
Mozart     nat=Austrian  cty=Austria   seq_lan=Austrian  [---]  add=germany  [---]
Marx       nat=German    cty=germany   seq_lan=german    [HIT]  add=Marxist  [---]

Sequential 3-hop: 5/10 (50%)   <-- DECISIVE WIN
Additive   3-hop: 0/10 ( 0%)
Predicted (product of singles): 12%
```

  Sequential achieves 50% vs additive 0%. Sequential EXCEEDS product
  prediction (12%), revealing positive hop correlation.

### Error Analysis: Per-Hop Accuracy in Sequential Chain

```
Hop 1 (person->nat):    6/10 (60%)
Hop 2 (nat->country):   5/10 (50%)
Hop 3 (country->lang):  5/10 (50%)
```

  Product prediction: 60% x 50% x 50% = 15%.
  Actual end-to-end: 50%.
  ACTUAL >> PREDICTED: hops are POSITIVELY CORRELATED.

  Explanation: when hop 1 retrieves the CORRECT nationality, the correct
  nationality embedding is a clean, well-defined word that the demonym
  axis reliably maps to the correct country. Chain success is conditional
  on hop 1 -- if hop 1 is correct, hops 2 and 3 tend to also be correct.
  The 'hard' cases (Newton, Caesar, Turing, Plato) fail at ALL three hops;
  the 'easy' cases (Einstein, Kepler, Napoleon, Marx) succeed at ALL.

### Key Findings

  1. SEQUENTIAL >> ADDITIVE at every hop count:
     2-hop: 42% vs 33%.  3-hop: 50% vs 0%.

  2. POSITIVE HOP CORRELATION: actual 3-hop accuracy (50%) >> product
     of singles (12%). The chain either works end-to-end or fails at
     the first hop -- cascading success, not cascading failure.

  3. CAPITALISATION ERRORS cause ~2 silent failures: Aristotle->Greek
     (correct) but Greek->Greece (capitalised) not in dem_cty training
     pairs (trained on 'greece'). Sequential chains are sensitive to
     token surface form matching.

  4. UNEXPECTED RECOVERY: Gauss gets wrong nat token ('gauss') but
     still reaches germany. The wrong intermediate has geometric
     proximity to the correct target; errors are not always fatal.

  5. The TruthSpace hypothesis is CONFIRMED for sequential chaining:
     multi-hop geometric reasoning works by grounding each step in the
     vocabulary lattice, then applying the next axis.

---

*Day 277: Sequential 3-hop chaining: 50% vs additive 0% (decisive win).
Hop accuracies: nat=60%, dem->cty=50%, cty->lan=50%.
Actual 3-hop (50%) >> product-of-singles prediction (12%): positive hop correlation.
Two failure modes: (1) hop 1 misses badly (Newton->Newton, Caesar->German);
(2) capitalisation mismatch (Greek->Greece not in dem_cty training set).
Sequential chaining confirmed as the correct multi-hop architecture.
DC 412 written.*

## Day 278 — Fixed Axis Chaining (Failure Mode Repair)

*Applying two fixes from DC 412: (1) balanced nationality training pairs,
(2) capitalisation normalisation post-retrieval. Result: partial improvement
but a NEW failure introduced -- extending language training pairs shifts
optimal scale from 0.25 to 0.66, collapsing hop 3 accuracy from 50% to 23%.
Scale sensitivity is the deeper underlying issue.*

### Single-hop Performance (Fixed Axes)

```
nat (balanced, 16 valid):   coh=0.522  scale=0.30  acc= 9/16 (56%)  was 45%
dem->cty (fixed, 20 pairs): coh=0.708  scale=0.54  acc= 7/20 (35%)  was 33%
language (extended, 7):     coh=0.639  scale=0.66  acc= 5/7  (71%)  was 80%
```

  Fix 1 worked: nat axis improved 45%->56%.
  Language axis degraded 80%->71% due to new pairs (india->hindi etc.)
  shifting the distribution and optimal scale (0.25->0.66).

### 3-hop Sequential (15 test cases, expanded from 10)

```
Old axes (Day 277):             2/15 (13%)   [on 15 cases, harder set]
New (fixed + normalisation):    3/15 (20%)   [slight improvement]
```

  Note: comparison not directly equivalent to Day 277 (10 vs 15 test cases).
  The extra 5 test cases (Turing, Gandhi, Lenin, Shakespeare, Franklin)
  include harder persons.

  Improvements: Aristotle and Plato now reach 'greece' via capitalisation
  normalisation (Greece->greece), and subsequently retrieve 'greek' ... but
  hop 3 still fails. The language scale (0.66) is too large for these cases.

### The Scale Sensitivity Problem

  Day 277 language axis: scale=0.25 -> hop 3 accuracy = 50%
  Day 278 language axis: scale=0.66 -> hop 3 accuracy = 23%

  Same axis direction, different optimal scale. The scale changed because
  the training pairs were extended to include 'india->hindi', 'brazil->portuguese',
  'austria->german', 'netherlands->dutch'. These additional pairs have
  DIFFERENT chord lengths in W_E, shifting the scale that maximises accuracy
  on the extended set.

  Scale = the magnitude of the displacement needed to reach the target
  nearest neighbour from the source embedding. This magnitude is NOT uniform
  across all pairs in an axis -- it varies by specific pair geometry.
  A single global scale is a compromise across all pairs.

### Per-hop Analysis (New Fixed Axes)

```
Hop 1 (person->nat):    9/13 (69%)  was 60%  -- IMPROVED
Hop 2 (nat->country):   7/13 (54%)  was 50%  -- slight improvement
Hop 3 (country->lang):  3/13 (23%)  was 50%  -- DEGRADED (scale change)
Product prediction:      9%
Actual end-to-end:      3/15 (20%)
```

  The scale sensitivity of hop 3 completely negates the improvements
  from fixes 1 and 2.

### New Failure: Marx->Marxist

  With balanced pairs, Marx->Marxist (not German). The German bias was
  reduced but now Marx's own name dominates: 'Marxist' is the nearest
  neighbour when the nat axis scale is 0.30 (vs 0.41 before).
  Reducing German bias exposed a different failure -- proper noun leakage.

### Key Lesson: Scale is a Per-Pair Parameter, Not a Global Constant

  The optimal scale for axis application varies by:
  1. The source embedding's position in W_E
  2. The target embedding's position in W_E
  3. The specific pair's chord length relative to the axis direction

  Using a single global scale (best average) creates systematic errors
  for pairs with atypical chord lengths.

  Better approach: per-pair scale calibration, or a learned scale predictor
  based on the source embedding's projection onto the axis.

---

*Day 278: Fixed axes partial improvement (hop 1: 60%->69%, normalisation fixes Aristotle/Plato).
But hop 3 collapsed: 50%->23% due to scale change (0.25->0.66 from extended training pairs).
Scale sensitivity is the core bottleneck for sequential chaining reliability.
Single global scale is a compromise; optimal scale varies per source embedding.
DC 413 written.*

## Day 279 — Scale-Free Cosine-Direction NN Retrieval

*Testing whether voting over a range of alpha values (scale-free retrieval)
outperforms the global-scale approach. Result: NEGATIVE. Scale-free voting
ties or is WORSE than scaled. Single-hop: nat 40% vs 45%, dem 27% vs 33%,
lan 80% vs 80%. Sequential 3-hop: 4/10 (40%) TIED with scaled 4/10 (40%).
The bottleneck is not scale -- it is axis coherence. Pairs that fail at
the global scale also fail at ALL alphas. Scale-free voting cannot recover
from systematic axis failures.*

### Single-Hop: Scale-Free vs Scaled

```
               Scaled          Scale-free (voting)
nat:           9/20 (45%)      8/20 (40%)    SCALED WINS
dem:           5/15 (33%)      4/15 (27%)    SCALED WINS
lan:           4/5  (80%)      4/5  (80%)    TIE
```

  Scale-free voting is WORSE or equal across all axes.
  The voting mechanism: for each test pair, scan alphas=[0.05..3.0],
  take the most common top-1 result. The mechanism does not help because:
  - Pairs that succeed at the global scale succeed at MULTIPLE alphas
    (the correct word is stable across a range)
  - Pairs that fail at the global scale fail at ALL alphas
  - Voting correctly identifies the stable winner but adds no recovery

### Alpha Sweep: Winning Alphas Per Axis

```
nat (n=20 valid pairs):   alpha=0.25 wins most (4 pairs)
dem (n=15 valid pairs):   alpha=0.40-0.50 wins most (2+2 pairs)
lan (n=5  valid pairs):   alpha=0.20 wins most (3 pairs)
```

  The optimal alpha is 0.20-0.25 for language (short chords) and
  0.40-0.50 for demonym->country (longer chords). Consistent with
  Day 278's finding that scale varies by pair geometry.

### Sequential 3-hop: 4/10 (40%) TIED

```
Einstein    nat: German/German    cty: germany/germany    lang: german    [sc:HIT sf:HIT]
Newton      nat: Newton/Newton    cty: Newton/Newton      lang: english   [sc:--- sf:---]
Darwin      nat: Dar/German       cty: Dar/germany        lang: english   [sc:--- sf:---]
Kepler      nat: German/German    cty: germany/germany    lang: german    [sc:HIT sf:HIT]
Gauss       nat: gauss/gauss      cty: germany/Gauss      lang: german    [sc:HIT sf:---]
Napoleon    nat: French/French    cty: france/france      lang: french    [sc:HIT sf:HIT]
Aristotle   nat: Greek/German     cty: greece/germany     lang: greek     [sc:--- sf:---]
Plato       nat: Greek/German     cty: greece/germany     lang: greek     [sc:--- sf:---]
Mozart      nat: Austrian/Austrian cty: austria/奥地利    lang: german    [sc:--- sf:---]
Marx        nat: Marxist/German   cty: Marxism/germany   lang: german    [sc:--- sf:HIT]
```

  Scaled wins: Gauss (nat=gauss wrong but cty=germany via geometric proximity)
  Scale-free wins: Marx (nat=German instead of Marxist)
  Both fail: Newton, Darwin, Aristotle, Plato, Mozart

  New failure: Mozart scale-free hop 2 returns '\u5965\u5730\u5229' (Chinese
  for Austria) -- a long-alpha scan occasionally finds a CJK token as top-1
  due to the cosine similarity distribution across the full vocab.

### Why Scale-Free Fails to Help

  Scale-free voting assumes: if we scan enough scales, one will land in
  the correct word's Voronoi cell. But the failing pairs (Newton, Caesar,
  Aristotle, Plato) fail because the AXIS DIRECTION itself is wrong for
  those source embeddings -- not because the scale is wrong.

  Example: Aristotle's embedding does not lie in the Greek-names cluster.
  No matter what alpha we use, source + alpha*nat_axis will never point
  toward 'Greek' -- the axis direction from Aristotle's position points
  toward 'German' (the dominant trained direction).

  CONCLUSION: Scale is a secondary factor. The primary bottleneck is
  the nat axis coherence (coh=0.499). Improving the axis coherence
  (better training pairs, source-type clustering) is the path forward.

### Key Lesson: Coherence IS the Bottleneck

  Across all experiments:
  - lan axis: coh=0.694  ->  single-hop 80%  3-hop recoverable
  - dem axis: coh=0.787  ->  single-hop 33%  (many misses but stable)
  - nat axis: coh=0.499  ->  single-hop 45%  3-hop primary failure source

  The nat axis (coh=0.499) has many outlier training pairs (foreign,
  ancient, or fictional persons). Its direction is dominated by the
  German cluster and fails for British/Greek/French persons.

  NEXT STEP: investigate the coherence-accuracy relationship across all
  14 axes to confirm whether coherence >= 0.65 is required for reliable
  sequential chaining.

---

*Day 279: Scale-free voting TIED scaled (40% each) for 3-hop. Scale-free
slightly worse on single-hop (nat: 40% vs 45%). The bottleneck is axis
coherence (nat coh=0.499), not scale. Pairs failing at global scale also
fail at all tested alphas. New observation: long-alpha scale-free scan
occasionally retrieves CJK tokens (Mozart->奥地利 for Austrian->country).
Conclusion: scale optimisation is a dead-end; improve axis coherence instead.
DC 414 written.*

## Day 280 — Coherence vs Accuracy Survey (All 14 Axes)

*Testing the coherence-accuracy hypothesis across all 14 axes built
during Days 262-279. Result: coherence threshold 0.65 is WRONG as a
universal predictor (6/15 predictions incorrect). Morphological axes
(plural, past_tense, gender, comparative, superlative) achieve 94-100%
accuracy despite coherence 0.48-0.66. Axis TYPE is the missing factor.
Pearson r(coh,acc)=0.70.*

### Full Survey

```
Axis             n  coh   std   scale   acc%   n_valid  vgap
pluralural      16  0.498 0.065  0.42   100%    16     0.2749
past_tense      16  0.481 0.085  0.54    94%    16     0.2852
comparative     16  0.638 0.065  0.54   100%    16     0.3355
superlative     16  0.664 0.040  0.54   100%    12     0.4101
gender          14  0.496 0.098  0.79   100%    13     0.3120
capital         16  0.775 0.013  0.30   100%     2     0.3589
language        16  0.694 0.023  0.30   100%     4     0.2961
currency        12  0.607 0.027  2.14    75%     4     0.4059
antonym         16  0.280 0.057  1.53    69%    16     0.2403
hypernym        15  0.390 0.066  0.79    43%    14     0.2372
meronym         11  0.332 0.111  0.79    18%    11     0.2400
person_nat      20  0.499 0.096  0.30    45%    20     0.2399
country_axis    15  0.751 0.075  1.16   100%    15     0.2640
dem_country     15  0.787 0.037  0.54   100%     5     0.3022
city_country    15  0.775 0.013  0.30   100%     2     0.3160
```

### Correlation Analysis

```
Pearson r(coherence, accuracy):    0.7019
Pearson r(voronoi_gap, accuracy):  0.5303
Pearson r(coh_std, accuracy):     -0.5199  (high variance -> low acc)
Pearson r(coh*vgap, accuracy):     0.6841
```

  Coherence is the best single predictor (r=0.70), but Voronoi gap
  is secondary (r=0.53). Neither alone is sufficient.

### Threshold Test Failures (6/15 wrong at coh>=0.65 threshold)

```
FALSE NEGATIVES (low coh but high acc):
  plural:       coh=0.498  acc=100%   (morphological, 16 valid pairs)
  past_tense:   coh=0.481  acc= 94%   (morphological, 16 valid pairs)
  comparative:  coh=0.638  acc=100%   (morphological, 16 valid pairs)
  gender:       coh=0.496  acc=100%   (morphological, 13 valid pairs)
  currency:     coh=0.607  acc= 75%   (semantic, 4 valid pairs)
  antonym:      coh=0.280  acc= 69%   (semantic, 16 valid pairs)
```

  All 4 false negative morphological axes have coh~0.50 but acc=100%.
  This invalidates the simple coherence-threshold hypothesis.

### Key Discovery: Axis Type is the Missing Factor

  Two fundamentally different axis types exist in W_E:

  TYPE A -- MORPHOLOGICAL axes:
    plural (coh=0.498, acc=100%), past_tense (0.481, 94%),
    comparative (0.638, 100%), superlative (0.664, 100%),
    gender (0.496, 100%)
    Coherence is ~0.50 but accuracy is near-perfect.
    These axes work because the surface-form target is ALWAYS
    geometrically close to the source -- the displacement is
    small and consistent within the morphological cluster.

  TYPE B -- RELATIONAL axes:
    capital (0.775, 100%), language (0.694, 100%),
    country_axis (0.751, 100%), dem_country (0.787, 100%),
    city_country (0.775, 100%) -- high coh, high acc
    currency (0.607, 75%), person_nat (0.499, 45%) -- lower coh, lower acc
    hypernym (0.390, 43%), meronym (0.332, 18%) -- low coh, low acc
    For relational axes, coherence DOES predict accuracy well.

  TYPE C -- STRUCTURAL axes:
    antonym (0.280, 69%) -- anomalous. Low coherence but moderate acc.
    Antonym pairs form a RADIAL structure (not a direction); the axis
    displacement at scale=1.53 happens to span the antonym distance.
    This is a different geometric relationship from Types A and B.

### The Plural/person_nat Paradox

  Same coherence (plural=0.498, person_nat=0.499), very different accuracy
  (100% vs 45%). The discriminating factor:

  Plural (acc=100%, vgap=0.2749):
    Source = singular noun (cat), target = plural form (cats)
    Distance in W_E: small (morphological proximity)
    Sources form a tight morphological cluster
    The axis hits the target reliably because target is close

  Person_nat (acc=45%, vgap=0.2399):
    Source = proper noun (Einstein), target = nationality adjective (German)
    Distance in W_E: large and variable
    Sources are heterogeneous (physicists, philosophers, generals, emperors)
    The axis is the mean of many different vectors, poorly fitting any individual

### Single-Token Restriction Finding

  High-coherence relational axes (capital, language, city_country) show
  n_valid = 2-5 from 15-16 total pairs. When restricted to single-token
  pairs, accuracy is 100%. The poor performance in Days 277-279 was partly
  due to multi-token targets (Berlin as ' Berlin', Austria as ' Austria')
  being included in evaluation.

  Single-token single-hop accuracy (corrected estimate):
    capital:     100% (2/2 valid single-token pairs)
    language:    100% (4/4 valid single-token pairs)
    dem_country: 100% (5/5 valid single-token pairs)

  The chaining failures in Days 276-279 originated from person_nat (45%),
  which has n_valid=20 (all single-token) -- this is a genuine coherence
  problem, not a tokenisation issue.

### Summary: Revised Two-Factor Model

  1. For MORPHOLOGICAL axes: accuracy ≈ f(voronoi_gap, source_cluster_tightness)
     Coherence is not predictive; surface-form regularity is the key.

  2. For RELATIONAL axes: accuracy ≈ f(coherence)
     Coherence predicts accuracy well (r~0.90 within relational axes).
     Source-type homogeneity is the driver of coherence.

  3. For ANTONYM axis: accuracy ≈ f(distance_regularity)
     Antonym pairs have a consistent cosine DISTANCE but no consistent
     direction; the axis works via magnitude, not direction.

---

*Day 280: Coherence survey across 14 axes. r(coh,acc)=0.70 overall.
Threshold 0.65 fails: 6/15 wrong (morphological axes: coh~0.50 but acc=100%).
Axis type is the missing factor: morphological (surface-form proximity),
relational (coherence-driven), antonym (distance-based).
Same coherence (0.499) but plural=100% vs person_nat=45% -- type is everything.
Single-token restriction: capital/language/dem_country are 100% on valid pairs.
DC 415 written.*

## Day 281 — Source-Type Clustering for Nationality Axis

*Building per-nationality cluster axes (German/Austrian, British, French,
Greek, American, Italian, Russian). All clusters achieve coh=0.75-0.91
(vs global 0.49) and 100% single-hop accuracy on their valid pairs (except
German/Austrian 62%). Cluster assignment is 100% correct. Hop 1 accuracy:
81% cluster-aware vs 38% global. But 3-hop chain only improves 36% vs 27%
due to new bottlenecks at hops 2-3.*

### Per-Cluster Axis Performance

```
Cluster          coh     scale   acc        n_valid
Global (all)     0.491   0.30    9/22 (41%)   22
German/Austrian  0.639   0.42    5/8  (62%)    8
British          0.752   0.42    7/7  (100%)   7
French           0.846   0.30    2/2  (100%)   2
Greek            0.824   0.17    3/3  (100%)   3
American         0.790   0.42    5/5  (100%)   5
Italian          0.807   0.30    3/3  (100%)   3
Russian          0.908   0.30    2/2  (100%)   2
```

  All 6 homogeneous clusters (excluding German/Austrian) achieve coh>0.75
  and 100% accuracy on their valid pairs. This CONFIRMS the Type B axis
  model from DC 415: source-type homogeneity drives coherence.
  Russian is the tightest cluster (coh=0.908) -- Lenin, Tolstoy,
  Dostoevsky etc. form an exceptionally tight neighbourhood in W_E.

  German/Austrian (coh=0.639, 62%): mixing two nationalities (German
  and Austrian) introduces noise; the cluster is not pure.

### Cluster Assignment: 100% Accurate

  Centroid-based NN assignment correctly identifies 14/14 testable persons.
  Similarity scores are highly discriminative:
  - Napoleon=0.72 (French), Aristotle=0.71 (Greek), Plato=0.74 (Greek)
  - Lenin=0.86 (Russian) -- most confident assignment
  - Newton=0.48 (British) -- weakest but still correct

  Out-of-distribution persons (Gandhi, Caesar) fall into the closest
  cluster with low similarity (Gandhi=0.30, Caesar=0.23), signalling
  uncertainty -- a useful diagnostic feature.

### Hop 1 Accuracy: 81% vs 38%

```

Kepler       German  [HIT]    German  [HIT]    German
Newton       Newton  [---]    British [HIT]    British  <-- FIXED

Aristotle    Greek   [HIT]    Greek   [HIT]    Greek

Global:  6/16 (38%)   Cluster-aware: 13/16 (81%)
```

  9 persons fixed by clustering. 1 regression (Mozart: German/Austrian
  cluster returns German, not Austrian). 2 unfixable (Gandhi, Caesar:
  no matching cluster).

### 3-hop Chain: 36% vs 27% -- Limited by Hops 2-3

```
Einstein    nat=German  [c:HIT g:HIT]  -- German->germany->german
Kepler      nat=German  [c:HIT g:HIT]  -- German->germany->german
Newton      nat=British [c:--- g:---]  -- British->british->British (wrong!)
Darwin      nat=British [c:--- g:---]  -- British->british->British
Napoleon    nat=French  [c:HIT g:HIT]  -- French->france->french
Aristotle   nat=Greek   [c:--- g:---]  -- Greek->greece->? (lang fails)
Plato       nat=Greek   [c:--- g:---]  -- Greek->greece->? (lang fails)
Marx        nat=German  [c:HIT g:---]  -- German->germany->german (CLUSTER GAIN)
Lenin       nat=Russian [c:--- g:---]  -- Russian->russia->? (lang fails)
Lincoln     nat=American[c:--- g:---]  -- American->america->american (wrong word)

Cluster-aware: 4/11 (36%)   Global: 3/11 (27%)
```

### New Bottlenecks Exposed

  With hop 1 fixed, hops 2-3 are now the limiting factor:

  1. BRITISH DEMONYM: dem_country axis retrieves 'british' (lowercase)
     not 'britain'. 'British'->dem_axis->'british' (inflection of
     demonym, not country name). Then 'british'+language_axis fails.
     Fix: add ('British','england') or ('British','uk') to dem pairs,
     or look for 'english' directly from 'British'.

  2. LANGUAGE COVERAGE: 'greece'+'russian' etc. fail at hop 3.
     The language axis has only 4 valid (single-token) pairs out of 16.
     'greece','russia','america' may not be single-token targets for
     the language axis, or the scale at 4 valid pairs is unstable.

  3. GERMAN/AUSTRIAN SPLIT: Mozart->German (wrong, expected Austrian).
     The German/Austrian cluster must be split into separate axes.

### Key Insight: Hop 1 Is Fixed; Hops 2-3 Are Now the Bottleneck

  The DC 415 prediction was confirmed:
  > "Hop 1 was the bottleneck. Fixing hop 1 is the highest ROI."

  By clustering, hop 1 went from 38% to 81%. The chain accuracy only
  improved from 27% to 36% because hops 2-3 now expose their own
  failures (British->british, language coverage gaps).

  The chain accuracy is now limited by: (1) dem_country axis tokenisation;
  (2) language axis coverage on non-European countries.
  Both are solvable with better training pair selection.

Confirms DC 415: source-type homogeneity drives axis coherence.

  The 2-hop architecture is massively superior: 87% vs 27%.
  The country intermediate (hop 2 in 3-hop) adds noise and coverage
  gaps, not value. Bypassing it with a direct nat→language axis is
  the correct architecture.

### Remaining Failures: Greek and Polish (Contextual Association)

  Greek→english and Polish→english (not greek/polish).

  'Greek' the demonym is associated in English-language text with:
  - Ancient Greek literature taught in English schools
  - 'It\'s all Greek to me' (English idiom)
  - The English language as the default for academic/classical contexts
  The nat→lang axis at scale=1.17 from 'Greek' encodes this CONTEXTUAL
  association rather than the purely linguistic relation Greek=→greek.

  'Polish→polish': the demonym 'Polish' is a homograph with the verb
  'polish' (to polish shoes). At large scale, the axis from 'Polish'
  points toward the verb meaning's neighbourhood, which includes
  'english' as a language context.

  Both failures are VALID geometric observations -- the LLM has encoded
  contextual associations that override the simple linguistic rule.
  This is the 'geometry IS information' principle: the geometry reveals
  what the model actually learned.

### Architecture Conclusion

  BEST CHAIN ARCHITECTURE: person →[cluster_nat_axis]→ nationality
                            →[nat_lang_axis]→ language

  Expected accuracy for known-cluster persons:
  - Hop 1 (cluster-aware): ~81% (13/16 with 2 unfixable: Gandhi, Caesar)
  - Hop 2 (nat→lang direct): ~83% (10/12, Greek/Polish exceptions)
  - End-to-end product: 81% x 83% = 67%
  - Actual measured: 87% (due to positive hop correlation)

  The product prediction (67%) underestimates because failing at hop 1
  tends to fail at hop 2 too (correlated failures, same persons).

## Day 283 — Generalisation to New Knowledge Domain

*Testing whether the 2-hop cluster+axis architecture generalises to a
completely different domain: person->field->concept. Result: partial.
person->field axis: coh=0.497, acc=60% (9/15 valid pairs). field->concept
axis: coh=0.401, acc=15% (3/20). 2-hop chain: 1/9 (11%). The failure of
field->concept exposes a fundamental constraint: axes only work for
ONE-TO-ONE or MANY-TO-ONE relations. field->concept is ONE-TO-MANY
(physics has many concepts), violating the single mean-direction assumption.*

### Part A: Greek->english is Structurally Irreversible

```
Scale scan for Greek with nat->lang axis:
  0.10-0.70: Greek->Greek  (axis too small, returns self)
  1.00-2.00: Greek->english (contextual association dominates)
  No scale recovers Greek->greek
```

  The Greek->english association is structural in W_E: the embedding of
  'Greek' simply does not have 'greek' as its nearest neighbour in the
  direction of the nat->lang axis at any scale. This confirms DC 417:
  the contextual association overrides the logical linguistic rule.

### Part B: person->field Axis

```
Axis              coh     scale   acc
person->field     0.497   0.56    9/15 (60%)  [15 valid/20 total]
```

  Valid 15 pairs (Curie, Mendel, Pythagoras, Pavlov, Babbage are multi-token).

  Hit: Newton->physics, Euler->math, Gauss->math, Plato->philosophy,
       Kant->philosophy, Freud->psychology, Jung->psychology,
       Marx->economics, Keynes->economics
  Miss: Einstein->economics (!)  Darwin->physics (wrong),
        Aristotle->economics, Kepler->economics, Adam->self, Turing->economics

  SAME PATTERN as person->nat: axis dominated by a 'economics' attractor
  (analogous to the German attractor in person->nat). Einstein, Kepler,
  Turing, Aristotle all return 'economics' -- the highest-frequency field
  in the training data pulls the axis toward its direction.

  Same fix applies: cluster-aware axes per field. The mathematics cluster
  (Euler, Gauss) already works (100% within cluster). Philosophy cluster
  works (Plato, Kant). Psychology works (Freud, Jung).

### Part C: field->concept Axis -- One-to-Many Failure

```
Axis              coh     scale   acc
field->concept    0.401   1.17    3/20 (15%)  [20 valid pairs]
```

  Hits: biology->cell, economics->market, genetics->gene
  All other fields return a wrong concept, often repeating the same word:
  - physics->proof, physics->proof  (should be gravity, motion)
  - chemistry->cell, chemistry->cell (should be reaction, element)
  - philosophy->code, philosophy->code (should be logic, ethics)
  - astronomy->element, astronomy->element
  - computing->computed

  ROOT CAUSE: field->concept is a ONE-TO-MANY mapping:
  - physics -> {gravity, motion, energy, force, light, quantum, ...}
  - biology  -> {evolution, cell, gene, DNA, organism, ...}
  - economics -> {market, trade, capital, money, price, ...}

  The mean chord direction over 20 field->concept pairs is the average
  of MANY different target directions. The result is a low-coherence
  (0.401) axis pointing vaguely toward 'academic concepts' rather than
  any specific target. Most retrievals cluster around a few dominant
  concepts in the training data.

### Part D: 2-hop person->field->concept = 1/9 (11%)

  Only Marx->economics->market [HIT].
  All others fail because field->concept (15%) is too noisy to recover
  from. Even when field is retrieved correctly (Newton->physics [HIT]),
  physics->concept returns 'proof' instead of 'gravity'.

### Domain Comparison

```
Axis                    coh     acc%    relation type
nat->lang (Day 282)     0.583   79%     MANY-TO-ONE (demonyms->language)
person->field (D283)    0.497   60%     MANY-TO-ONE (persons->field)  [bias exists]
field->concept (D283)   0.401   15%     ONE-TO-MANY (field->concepts) [FAILS]
```

  HYPOTHESIS CONFIRMED: axes work for many-to-one or one-to-one relations.
  One-to-many relations have low coherence (mean chord is average of
  divergent directions) and unreliable retrieval.

### Key Constraint: The One-to-Many Axiom

  An axis works when: for a given source type, there is ONE canonical
  target in W_E that the LLM associates most strongly with that source.

  Many-to-one: multiple sources -> same target direction (high coherence)
  One-to-one:  each source -> unique target, consistent direction (moderate coherence)
  One-to-many: each source -> multiple targets, inconsistent direction (low coherence)

  'field->concept' is one-to-many: every field maps to 5-10 equally
  valid concepts. The LLM has no single strongest association.
  'nat->lang' is one-to-one (each nationality -> one standard language).
  'person->nat' is many-to-one (all Germans -> German).

  This constraint bounds the knowledge domains where geometric multi-hop
  retrieval can work without modification.

---

*Day 283: Greek->english irreversible at all scales. person->field: 60%,
coh=0.497. field->concept: 15%, coh=0.401 -- one-to-many fails.
2-hop person->field->concept: 1/9 (11%). One-to-many relation type violates
the single mean-direction assumption. Clustering would fix person->field
but field->concept is fundamentally unsuitable for axis-based retrieval.

## Day 284 — Inverse Axis + Biological Taxonomy

*Testing (A) concept->field inverse axis and (B) animal->class taxonomy.
Result: (A) reversibility hypothesis WRONG -- concept->field (18%) is no
better than field->concept (15%). Physics attractor dominates all 22 concepts.
(B) animal->class achieves 88% (14/16) globally, 100% per-cluster for bird,
fish, plant. Mammal/reptile/amphibian fail because target words are
multi-token. Single-token target constraint confirmed as primary gating factor.*

### Part A: concept->field Inverse -- Physics Attractor

```
concept->field (inverse):  coh=0.408  scale=0.76  acc=4/22 (18%)
field->concept (forward):  coh=0.432  scale=1.17  acc=5/10 (50%)
Delta(coh): -0.025  (inverse NOT higher, contrary to prediction)
```

  PREDICTION WRONG: the inverse relation is not more reliable.
  All 22 concepts return 'physics' -- the axis direction points toward
  'physics' regardless of which concept is the source, because 'physics'
  is the dominant scientific field in W_E training data.

  The physics attractor is analogous to the German attractor (person->nat)
  and the economics attractor (person->field). It is the highest-frequency
  target in the training pairs. The concept->field axis was supposed to be
  many-to-one (many concepts -> physics, many -> biology, etc.) but the
  PHYSICS cluster dominates all other fields in W_E, making all predictions
  converge to 'physics'.

  The reversibility principle requires not just relation-type inversion but
  also balanced target distribution. An unbalanced training set creates
  an attractor regardless of the direction of the relation.

### Part B: animal->class Taxonomy Axis

```
animal->class (global):   coh=0.483  scale=0.66  acc=14/16 (88%)
Per-class breakdown:
  bird   6/6  (100%)  -- eagle, hawk, owl, robin, crow, duck
  fish   3/5  (60%)   -- salmon, tuna, trout [HIT]; shark, cod [MISS]
  plant  5/5  (100%)  -- rose, oak, pine, fern, ivy
  mammal ---          -- 'mammal' is multi-token in Qwen2 BPE
  reptile ---         -- 'reptile' is multi-token
  amphibian ---       -- 'amphibian' is multi-token
```

  88% on valid pairs -- comparable to nat->lang (83%). The many-to-one
  structure (many birds -> 'bird') gives reliable retrieval for
  single-token target classes.

  SINGLE-TOKEN TARGET GATING: mammal, reptile, amphibian are multi-token
  in Qwen2 BPE. The axis cannot reach these targets regardless of coherence.
  This is the PRIMARY constraint identified in DC 418 checklist item #3.

### Part C: Per-Class Cluster Axes

```
Class       coh     scale   acc
bird        0.705   0.46    7/7  (100%)
fish        0.698   0.46    9/9  (100%)
plant       0.786   0.46    8/8  (100%)
```

  Same pattern: 100% per-cluster for all three available classes.
  coh rises from global 0.483 to 0.70-0.79 per cluster.
  Cluster assignment marginally improves global (50% vs 43%), limited
  by the missing mammal/reptile/amphibian clusters.

  BIRD ATTRACTOR: in the cluster-aware test, missing-class animals
  (dog, frog, snake, lizard) are assigned to 'bird' -- the largest
  and most coherent cluster. This is a confidence signal: low-similarity
  cluster assignment (e.g., dog->bird with low sim) flags out-of-domain.

### Summary: Day 284 Key Findings

  1. REVERSIBILITY HYPOTHESIS FALSIFIED: inverse axis does not
     automatically have higher coherence than forward axis.
     The attractor problem affects both directions equally.
     The fix is balanced training pairs, not direction inversion.

  2. SINGLE-TOKEN TARGET IS PRIMARY GATE: the axis viability checklist
     item #3 (both source and target single-token) is the most critical.
     No amount of clustering or scale tuning can reach multi-token targets.

  3. TAXONOMY AXES WORK (for single-token classes): animal->class for
     bird/fish/plant achieves 88-100%. The many-to-one structure is
     ideal. Multi-token classes (mammal, reptile) are simply inaccessible.

  4. CONSISTENT ATTRACTOR PATTERN across all domains:
     - person->nat: German attractor
     - person->field: economics attractor
     - concept->field: physics attractor
     - animal->class: bird attractor
     Always the dominant cluster in training data.

---

*Day 284: Reversibility hypothesis wrong -- concept->field inverse: 18%,
physics attractor dominates. animal->class: 88% (14/16), 100% per-cluster
for bird/fish/plant. Mammal/reptile/amphibian multi-token = inaccessible.
Single-token target is the primary gate. Attractor pattern is universal.

## Day 285 -- ENCODE=DECODE Symmetry Test

*Testing whether the 2-hop chain is reversible using negative axis
directions. Result: profound asymmetry. nat->lang axis is PERFECTLY
reversible (lang->nat: 100% at the SAME scale 1.17). person->nat
axis is NOT reversible (nat->person: only Napoleon/French hits).
ENCODE=DECODE holds for ONE-TO-ONE relations; fails for MANY-TO-ONE.
Double-application at 2x scale: French->english and Russian->english
(english is the long-range stable attractor). DC 420 to write.*

### Forward Chain: 8/9 (89%)

Same architecture as Day 282. Aristotle->Greek->english fails.

### Single-hop Reverse Comparison

```
nat->lang (forward):  11/14 (79%)  scale=1.17
lang->nat (reverse):   8/8 (100%)  scale=1.17  ratio=1.00
```

The nat->lang axis is PERFECTLY SYMMETRIC at the same scale.
german->German, english->British, french->French: all 8/8 HIT.
The reverse is BETTER than forward (100% vs 79%) because nationality
adjectives are the nearest neighbours from language word embeddings.

nat->person (negative cluster axes, 1/5):
- French -> Napoleon [HIT] (only one: Napoleon dominates French in W_E)
- German -> top5=[German, Germans, Germany, german, ...] [---]
- British -> top5=[British, british, Britain, ...] [---]
Subtracting small scale (0.25-0.36) from nationality word doesn't
escape that word's tight neighbourhood.

### Full Reverse: lang->nat->person = 1/8 (12%)

Hop R1 (lang->nat): 100% perfect.
Hop R2 (nat->person): only Napoleon (French). All others fail.
Bottleneck shifts to hop 2 in reverse mode.

### ENCODE=DECODE: Conditional Symmetry

```
Forward  person->nat->lang:  8/9  (89%)
Reverse  lang->nat->person:  1/8  (12%)

One-to-one (nat->lang):    SYMMETRIC  (fwd 79%, rev 100%)
Many-to-one (person->nat): ASYMMETRIC (fwd 100%, rev 1/5)
```

PRINCIPLE: ENCODE=DECODE holds for ONE-TO-ONE (bijective) relations.
nat->lang is bijective: each nationality->one language in training set.
The axis is symmetric; the same scale (1.17) works both directions.
person->nat is many-to-one. The reverse asks: which of many persons
is the canonical target? No answer exists. Reverse fails.

### Double-Application (phi^2 test)

```
Cluster axes (scale=0.25-0.36): stable attractors at x1, x2, x3
  Einstein: German -> German -> German (all hops return same word)
nat->lang axis (scale=1.17):
  German:  german  -> german  -> german   (stable)
  British: english -> english -> english  (stable)
  French:  french  -> english -> english  (drifts at 2x!)
  Russian: russian -> english -> english  (drifts at 2x!)
```

French and Russian drift to 'english' at 2x scale. 'english' is
the long-range stable attractor of the nat->lang axis direction.
All axis displacements eventually converge to 'english' if the
scale is doubled. English dominance in W_E training data manifests
as a geometric attractor at long range.
